challenge: Mithra Whole Foods sells chemical-free traditional foods — millets, cold-pressed oils, ghee, jaggery — and it was running on an ageing template store that didn't feel premium, couldn't be extended, and needed a developer for every banner change.
The rebuild had to keep the full commerce path working end to end, stay cheap to run for a small brand, and hand day-to-day content back to the client.
architectureCaption: A Next.js storefront on Vercel talks to a Medusa v2 backend on Railway, which owns the data in Neon Postgres and takes payments through Stripe.

steps.title: Browse
steps.desc: Category and product pages render from the Medusa Store API, with real product photography and the client's own wordmark traced to SVG.

steps.title: Search
steps.desc: /store/search runs inside the backend and returns product ids — no Meilisearch or Algolia to host, pay for or keep in sync.

steps.title: Add to cart
steps.desc: The cart context applies a local change first, reconciles with the backend, and rolls back with a toast if the backend rejects it.

steps.title: Check out
steps.desc: Address → shipping → payment → review, with Stripe through Medusa's payment provider and an order confirmation at the end.

steps.title: Edit the homepage
steps.desc: A custom homepage module with an admin live-preview page lets the client change banners and featured collections without a deploy.

decisions.title: Headless, on an open-source commerce core
decisions.desc: Medusa v2 provides orders, carts, customers and payments as a backend; the storefront is free to look like the brand instead of a template.

decisions.title: Search without a search service
decisions.desc: Meilisearch was removed in favour of an in-house search endpoint. For a catalogue this size it's fast enough, free, and has nothing to keep in sync.

decisions.title: Optimistic, but honest
decisions.desc: The cart feels instant, but the backend is the source of truth — a rejected change rolls back visibly instead of silently drifting.

decisions.title: Measure before migrating
decisions.desc: A slow store prompted 'should we move to Supabase?'. Measuring showed ~290 ms per query from the backend–database distance; a same-region link is 1–3 ms. The answer was region, not vendor.

roadmap: Co-locate the backend and database in one region to remove the ~290 ms per-query penalty.
Switch on the analytics and observability that are already built, then fix correctness gaps they surface.
Shipping automation through the Easyship fulfilment module.
Bring the UI back in line with the defined design system.
